Here's my initial advice on the Harbor Relay US pilot.

Initial advice — Harbor Relay account activity report

What you've told me: A US pilot of Harbor Relay launches 21 October 2026. The product sends an account activity report to the customer, retained 30 days, and the supplied spec says only the customer can open it. Business hasn't confirmed whether support staff can open reports. Working assessment (preliminary, no authority retrieved): The report almost certainly contains customer transaction/account data, so the two design choices you've flagged — 30-day retention and customer-only access — are privacy and data-access controls, not just product features. The material question is whether the "only the customer can open" statement is an accurate description of the product's actual access model.

If support staff can open reports, then the spec's "only the customer can open them" is inaccurate as written, and you'd want to reconcile it before the pilot. That's not necessarily a blocker — support access under defined conditions (e.g., a verified customer request or troubleshooting) is common and defensible — but the spec and any customer-facing disclosure should reflect the real access model. Unrestricted support access would be the harder position, since it undercuts the customer-only promise and widens exposure of customer data.
If support cannot open reports, the spec is accurate and the main remaining item is confirming the 30-day retention is deliberate (data minimization) and documented. The one supporting question that matters most is the support-access one, because it determines whether the stated access promise is accurate and whether additional controls or disclosures are needed before launch:

Can support staff open customer account activity reports, and if so under what conditions?

No — only the customer can open reports; support cannot
Yes — support can open reports only under defined conditions (e.g., verified customer request, troubleshooting)
Yes — support can open reports without restriction
Not yet decided — business is still determining this I've recorded the reported facts and this question in the matter. Per your instruction, I have not recorded a legal decision or created a draft. Once you answer the support-access question, I can give a more concrete read on what (if anything) needs to change in the spec or disclosures before the pilot.

Here is my assessment of the selected original advice against the supplied specification versions. No facts, decisions, or drafts have been changed — no draft exists yet.

What the supplied versions say (literal)

Spec v1 (source the internal record): retention 30 days; access "only the customer can open account activity reports"; "Support staff cannot open report content." Spec v2 (source the internal record): retention 180 days; access "customers and support staff can open account activity reports"; "Support access requires a customer support ticket and is logged." The two changed passages (PASS-67775a61a1c4f5a7391a, PASS-e3b51b13ca9f5280bf0a) show exactly these edits: version label, retention 30→180 days, and the access model from customer-only/no-support to customer-plus-support with ticket-gated, logged support access.

What the original advice assumed (generated significance, not supplied)

The saved advice (the internal record) was written against the v1 facts: 30-day retention, customer-only access, support access unconfirmed. It treated the "only the customer can open" statement as a product/contractual access promise and flagged the support-access question as the deciding factor. That framing was reasonable on the v1 record.

What changes under v2
Retention 30 → 180 days. The original advice treated 30-day retention as a data-minimization point to confirm as deliberate. Under v2, retention is six times longer. That is a materially different data-retention posture and should be reviewed on its own — why 180 days, what drives the longer window, and whether it is consistent with any data-minimization or deletion commitments. The original advice did not address a 180-day window.
Support access is now specified, not unconfirmed. The original advice's central open question — "Can support staff open reports, and under what conditions?" — is answered by v2: yes, but only for a customer support ticket, and logged. This matches the reported fact from Sam Patel (the internal record) that support can open a report only for a customer support ticket with every access logged. So v2 and the reported business reply are now consistent with each other — a notable change from the v1 record, where the spec ("support cannot open") and Sam Patel's report conflicted.
The customer-only promise is gone. v2 no longer says "only the customer can open." It affirmatively states customers and support staff can open reports. So the original advice's premise that the spec's customer-only statement needed reconciling with support access is now moot at the spec level — v2 has already reconciled it by changing the access statement. The open working assumption the internal record (that the "only the customer can open" statement is a promise needing reconciliation) is now based on a superseded spec version.
What remains supported
The pilot date (21 Oct 2026), the product sending an account activity report to the customer, and the US-only scope are unchanged across both versions and remain supported.
The core privacy/data-access framing still holds: the report contains customer transaction/account data (assumption the internal record), so access to it implicates privacy and data-protection commitments. That is not undermined by v2 — if anything, the longer retention and broader (support) access make the data-access and retention controls more, not less, material.
The reported fact that support access is ticket-only and logged (the internal record) is now consistent with the v2 spec, which strengthens its plausibility as the intended model — though it remains reported, not independently verified.
What may need review
The 180-day retention is the biggest new item. It was not part of the original advice and should be reviewed on its own merits: the business rationale, consistency with any deletion/data-minimization commitments, and whether the longer window is disclosed or needs to be.
The access statement's accuracy. v2 says customers and support staff can open reports, with ticket-gated, logged support access. If that is the intended model, the earlier "only the customer can open" language is superseded, and any customer-facing disclosure should reflect the new access model. Whether the ticket-gating and logging are sufficient controls is a review point, not a settled conclusion.
The open supporting question. The support-access question (Q-support-access) is effectively answered by the combination of v2 and Sam Patel's report. The remaining open item is confirming the 180-day retention and whether the v2 access model is final.
Uncertainty preserved
Both spec versions are supplied specification text, not verified actual facts. The facts in the matter remain at "reported" status. v2 supersedes v1 as the current supplied spec, but that does not make the 180-day retention or the support-access model verified — it means the current supplied specification says so.
I have not confirmed why retention changed to 180 days, whether the ticket-gating/logging is implemented as described, or whether the v2 access model is final. Those remain open.
No external authority was retrieved; this is analysis of the supplied material only. Bottom line: The original advice was sound on the v1 record but is now partly superseded. The support-access question it centered on is answered by v2 (ticket-only, logged support access, consistent with Sam Patel's report), and the customer-only premise no longer holds. The material new item needing review is the 30→180-day retention change, which the original advice did not address. All facts, decisions, and drafts remain unchanged.
